meaning: A departure from what is normal, usual, or expected.
example: The sudden drop in temperature was an aberration in an otherwise mild winter.
tip: “Ab-” means away. Something that wandered away from the normal path.

meaning: Difficult to understand; obscure and deeply theoretical.
example: Her paper on quantum decoherence was too abstruse for a general audience.
tip: Rhymes with “obtuse” — a topic so dense it feels blunt against the mind.

meaning: An award or expression of high praise.
example: The film collected accolades at every festival it entered.
tip: Picture a cold ladle of praise being poured over the winner.

meaning: Keen insight and sharp judgment in practical matters.
example: Her business acumen turned a small shop into a national chain.
tip: “Acu-” means sharp, as in acupuncture. A sharp mind.

meaning: To warn or scold someone firmly but not harshly.
example: The professor admonished the class for submitting work late.
tip: Ad + monish: to add a warning, like a monitor.

meaning: To make suffering or a problem less severe.
example: Aspirin alleviates pain but does not cure the illness.
tip: A-LEVI-ate: it levitates the weight off your shoulders.

meaning: Open to more than one interpretation; unclear.
example: The survey question was ambiguous, so the answers were useless.
tip: “Ambi-” means both, as in ambidextrous. It can go both ways.

meaning: Something that deviates from what is standard or expected.
example: The instrument recorded an anomaly in the planet's orbit.
tip: A-nomaly = not normal.

meaning: Based on random choice or personal whim rather than reason.
example: The deadline felt arbitrary — no one could explain why it was Friday.
tip: An arbiter who decides by whim instead of by rule.

meaning: To express an idea clearly and effectively in words.
example: She articulated the team's concerns in a single sentence.
tip: Joints are articulated — clear connections between parts, like clear speech.

meaning: To make something greater by adding to it.
example: The university augmented its budget with private donations.
tip: Augmented reality adds layers on top of what is already there.

meaning: Kind, generous, and wishing others well.
example: A benevolent donor funded the entire scholarship program.
tip: “Bene” means good, as in benefit. Good-willed.

meaning: Honest and direct, even when the truth is uncomfortable.
example: He gave a candid assessment of the project's chances.
tip: A candid camera catches you completely unfiltered.

meaning: Something that causes or speeds up change without being changed itself.
example: The protest became a catalyst for constitutional reform.
tip: In chemistry it speeds reactions; in essays it speeds events.

meaning: To come together and form one whole.
example: The scattered groups coalesced into a single political movement.
tip: Co- (together) + alesce (grow): to grow together.

meaning: Clear, logical, and highly convincing.
example: She made a cogent case for delaying the launch.
tip: Close to “cogitate” (to think) — an argument built by real thinking.

meaning: Making a particular outcome likely or easy to achieve.
example: Silence is conducive to deep concentration.
tip: It conducts you toward the result.

meaning: An idea or feeling a word suggests beyond its literal meaning.
example: “Cheap” and “affordable” mean the same thing but carry different connotations.
tip: Con-note: the extra note played alongside the main meaning.

meaning: General agreement across a group.
example: The committee reached a consensus after three hours.
tip: Con + sense: everyone senses it the same way.

meaning: Clearly visible; attracting attention.
example: His absence at the ceremony was conspicuous.
tip: Con + spic (to look): everybody looks at it.

meaning: To confirm or support a statement with evidence.
example: Satellite images corroborated the researcher's claim.
tip: Co-ROBUST-erate: you make someone else's claim more robust.

meaning: Causing harm or damage, often gradually.
example: Deleterious effects of the pesticide appeared only after a decade.
tip: DELETE-erious: it slowly deletes what was healthy.

meaning: To represent or show something in a picture or in words.
example: The mural depicts the city as it looked in 1890.
tip: De + PICT(ure): to picture it.

meaning: To become progressively worse.
example: Air quality deteriorated sharply during the drought.
tip: De-TERRIBLE-ate: moving steadily toward terrible.

meaning: To perceive or recognize something that is not obvious.
example: It is hard to discern the author's true position from this passage.
tip: Dis + cern (to sift): sifting the signal out of the noise.

meaning: Fundamentally different in kind; not really comparable.
example: The theory tries to unite two disparate fields of study.
tip: Not “desperate.” DIS-PAIR-ate: things that refuse to pair up.

meaning: Asserting beliefs as absolute truth without accepting question.
example: His dogmatic tone shut down the discussion.
tip: A dog that will not let go of the bone.

meaning: Drawing from a wide and varied range of sources.
example: Her eclectic taste in music ranges from opera to grime.
tip: E-CLICK-tic: you click and collect from everywhere.

meaning: To draw out a response, answer, or reaction from someone.
example: The image elicited strong reactions from every participant.
tip: Not “illicit” (illegal). Elicit pulls something out into the light.

meaning: Based on observation or experiment rather than theory.
example: There is little empirical support for the hypothesis.
tip: An empire is built on land actually taken, not land imagined.

meaning: Lasting for a very short time.
example: Cherry blossoms are prized precisely because they are ephemeral.
tip: From Greek epi + hemera: lasting a single day.

meaning: To make a bad situation worse.
example: Cutting the budget only exacerbated the staffing shortage.
tip: Ex-ACERB-ate: pouring acid into an existing wound.

meaning: To make a process easier or help it happen.
example: A neutral moderator facilitated the negotiation.
tip: “Facile” means easy. To make easy.

meaning: Possible to do successfully with the means available.
example: Building the bridge is feasible but expensive.
tip: If you can feed it enough resources, it can be done.

meaning: To rise and fall irregularly.
example: Exchange rates fluctuated wildly all quarter.
tip: Shares a root with “flux” — flowing back and forth.

meaning: A system in which people or things are ranked in levels.
example: The company flattened its hierarchy to speed up decisions.
tip: “Hier” means sacred; originally the ranking of priests.

meaning: A proposed explanation that can be tested.
example: Their hypothesis was elegant but the data disproved it.
tip: “Hypo” means under: the idea placed under the experiment to be tested.

meaning: To slow down or block progress.
example: Heavy fog impeded the rescue effort.
tip: Im + PED (foot): something at your feet tripping you up.

meaning: Existing as a natural, inseparable part of something.
example: There are risks inherent in any clinical trial.
tip: It inherits the quality at birth — you cannot remove it.

meaning: Introducing new methods or ideas.
example: An innovative filter cut water costs by half.
tip: In + NOVA (new): bringing in the new.

meaning: Very detailed and complicated in structure.
example: The intricate carvings took a decade to complete.
tip: In + TRICK: so many small tricks woven together.

meaning: Producing a great deal of profit.
example: Consulting proved more lucrative than teaching.
tip: “Lucre” is an old word for money.

meaning: Showing extreme care about small details.
example: Her meticulous notes made the experiment reproducible.
tip: So careful they would notice a single meter out of place.

meaning: To reduce the severity of something harmful.
example: Sea walls mitigate flood damage but cannot prevent it.
tip: Do not confuse with “militate.” Mitigate makes a problem mite-sized.

meaning: New, original, and unlike anything before it.
example: The team proposed a novel approach to carbon capture.
tip: A classic TOEFL trap: here it is an adjective meaning new, not a book.

meaning: A very small difference in meaning, tone, or feeling.
example: Translation often loses the nuance of the original.
tip: From French “nue” (cloud): a tiny cloud passing over the meaning.

meaning: No longer in use because something better exists.
example: Fax machines became obsolete within a decade.
tip: OB-SO-LATE: so late that it is out of date.

meaning: A typical model or framework for how something works.
example: Plate tectonics created a new paradigm in geology.
tip: A para-diagram: the master diagram everyone works from.

meaning: On the edge; of minor importance to the main issue.
example: Cost was a peripheral concern next to safety.
tip: Computer peripherals sit around the edge of the main machine.

meaning: Seeming reasonable or probably true.
example: That is a plausible explanation, though it remains unproven.
tip: Related to “applause”: an idea you would clap for, even without proof.

meaning: Dealing with things practically rather than theoretically.
example: She took a pragmatic view: fix what can be fixed now.
tip: A program that actually runs, not one that only looks good.

meaning: An earlier event or decision used as a guide for later ones.
example: The ruling set a precedent for future privacy cases.
tip: What precedes becomes the rule for what follows.

meaning: To increase rapidly in number.
example: Coral bleaching allowed algae to proliferate.
tip: PROLIFIC + rate: reproducing at speed.

meaning: Producing a great deal of work or output.
example: A prolific composer, she wrote over 400 pieces.
tip: PRO-LIFE-ic: bringing a great many things to life.

meaning: Unnecessary because it repeats something already present.
example: Cut the redundant phrase “past history.”
tip: Waves of the same thing rolling over you again and again.

meaning: Able to recover quickly from difficulty.
example: Mangrove forests are remarkably resilient after storms.
tip: Re-SILENT: it bounces back without complaining.

meaning: To examine closely and critically.
example: Auditors scrutinized every line of the report.
tip: Look so hard you could screw your eyes right in.

meaning: Coming after something else in time.
example: Subsequent studies failed to replicate the finding.
tip: Sub + sequence: next in the sequence.

meaning: To provide evidence that proves something is true.
example: He could not substantiate his claim about the artifact's age.
tip: Give it substance — turn a loose claim into something solid.

meaning: Real and concrete enough to be perceived or measured.
example: The program produced tangible improvements in literacy.
tip: “Tang” means touch, as in tactile. You can touch it.

meaning: Very weak or slight; easily broken.
example: The link between the two events is tenuous at best.
tip: Thin as a ten-denier thread.

meaning: Present or found everywhere.
example: Smartphones are now ubiquitous in classrooms.
tip: U-BI-QUIT: you cannot quit it, because it is everywhere.

meaning: To weaken something gradually from below.
example: Poor record-keeping undermined the study's credibility.
tip: Digging a mine under a wall until the wall falls.

meaning: Capable of working successfully or surviving.
example: Solar became a viable alternative once prices fell.
tip: “Via” relates to life, as in vital. It has enough life to succeed.
